<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
The functional $\omega_2:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)\to[0,\infty)$ enjoys the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $\omega_2(T)\geq0$, ~$\omega_2(T)=0\iff T=O$.
\item[(ii)] $\omega_2(\lambda T)=|\lambda|\omega_2(T)$, $ \lambda\in\mathbb{C}$.
\item[(iii)] $\omega_2(S+T)\leq\omega_2(S)+\omega_2(T)$.
\item[(iv)] $\omega_2(U^*TU)=\omega_2(T)$, for every unitary operator $U$ (i.e., $U^*U=UU^*=I$, where \(I\) is the identity operator on \(\mathcal H\)).
\item [(v)] $\omega_2(e^{i\phi}T)=\omega_2(T)$ and $\omega_2(T^*)=\omega_2(T)$ for every $\phi\in\mathbb{R}$.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
\hfill

(i) Nonnegativity is immediate. Suppose $\omega_2(T)=0$. The function
\[
\theta\longmapsto
\left\lVert \cos\theta H+\sin\theta K\right\rVert^2
\]
is continuous and nonnegative, so it must vanish identically. Taking
$\theta=0$ and $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $H=O$ and $K=O$, hence $T=O$.

(ii) Let $\lambda=re^{i\phi}$, where $r=|\lambda|$. The Cartesian
components of $\lambda T$ are
\[
H_\lambda=r(\cos\phi\,H-\sin\phi\,K),
\qquad
K_\lambda=r(\sin\phi\,H+\cos\phi\,K).
\]
Therefore
\[
\cos\theta H_\lambda+\sin\theta K_\lambda
=
r\bigl(\cos(\theta-\phi)H+\sin(\theta-\phi)K\bigr).
\]
After the change of variable $u=\theta-\phi$,
\[
\omega_2(\lambda T)^2
=r^2\omega_2(T)^2,
\]
and hence
\[
\omega_2(\lambda T)=|\lambda|\omega_2(T).
\]

(iii) If
\[
S=H_S+iK_S,\qquad T=H_T+iK_T,
\]
then
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left\lVert \cos\theta(H_S+H_T)+
\sin\theta(K_S+K_T)\right\rVert\\
&\leq
\left\lVert \cos\theta H_S+\sin\theta K_S\right\rVert
+
\left\lVert \cos\theta H_T+\sin\theta K_T\right\rVert.
\end{aligned}
\]
Applying Minkowski's inequality in $L^2([0,2\pi])$ gives
\[
\omega_2(S+T)\leq\omega_2(S)+\omega_2(T).
\]

(iv) The Cartesian decomposition of $U^*TU$ is
\[
U^*TU=U^*HU+iU^*KU.
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_2(U^*TU)^2
&=
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
\left\lVert U^*(\cos\theta H+\sin\theta K)U\right\rVert^2\,d\theta\\
&=
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
\left\lVert \cos\theta H+\sin\theta K\right\rVert^2\,d\theta\\
&=\omega_2(T)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

(v) The first assertion follows from the homogeneity proof above with
$|\lambda|=1$. For the second, the Cartesian decomposition of $T^*$ is
$H-iK$, and hence
\[
\omega_2(T^*)^2
=
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
\left\lVert \cos\theta H-\sin\theta K\right\rVert^2\,d\theta.
\]
The substitution $\theta\mapsto-\theta$ proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{3}
Let $T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. If $T=T^*$, then
\[\omega_2(T)=\frac1{\sqrt2}\left\lVert T\right\rVert =\frac1{\sqrt2}\omega(T).\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
In this case $K=O$, so
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
=
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\,\left\lVert T\right\rVert^2
=
\frac12\left\lVert T\right\rVert^2.
\]
Since $\omega(T)=\left\lVert T\right\rVert$ for self-adjoint operators, the result follows.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{4}
Let $T=H+iK\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. If
\[
H^2=K^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
HK+KH=O,
\]
then
\[\omega(T)=\omega_2(T)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert^{1/2}.\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Under the assumptions, we know that
\[
H^2-K^2=O
\]
and
\[
HK+KH=O.
\]
Therefore
\[
A_\theta^2
=
\frac12(H^2+K^2)
\]
for every $\theta$.
Hence
\[
\left\lVert A_\theta\right\rVert^2
=
\frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert
\]
for every $\theta$. Thus
\[
\omega(T)^2
=
\sup_\theta\left\lVert A_\theta\right\rVert^2
=
\frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert.
\]
Also,
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}
\int_0^{2\pi}\left\lVert A_\theta\right\rVert^2\,d\theta
=
\frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert.
\]
Therefore
\[
\omega(T)^2=\omega_2(T)^2.
\]
Taking square roots proves the result.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{5}
Let $T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then
\[\frac1{\sqrt2}\omega(T) \leq \omega_2(T) \leq \omega(T).\]
Both constants are sharp.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By the Cartesian characterization of $\omega(T)$, we have
\[
\left\lVert \cos\theta H+\sin\theta K\right\rVert\leq \omega(T)
\]
for every $\theta$. Hence
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
\leq
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\omega(T)^2\,d\theta
=\omega(T)^2.
\]
Therefore $\omega_2(T)\leq \omega(T)$.

For the lower bound, let $x\in\mathcal H$ be a unit vector and put
\[
a=\left\langle Hx,x\right\rangle,\qquad b=\left\langle Kx,x\right\rangle.
\]
Then
\[
\left\langle Tx,x\right\rangle=a+ib.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_2(T)^2
&\geq
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
|a\cos\theta+b\sin\theta|^2\,d\theta\\
&=
\frac12(a^2+b^2)\\
&=\frac12|\left\langle Tx,x\right\rangle|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the supremum over all unit vectors $x$ yields
\[
\omega_2(T)^2\geq\frac12\omega(T)^2,
\]
and hence
\[
\omega_2(T)\geq\frac1{\sqrt2}\omega(T).
\]

To see sharpness, let $T=T^*\neq O$. Then $K=O$ and, according to Proposition \ref{3}, we have
\[
\omega_2(T)=\frac1{\sqrt2}\omega(T).
\]
The upper constant $1$ is also sharp. To see this, let
\[
 H=
 \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 K=
 \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},
 \qquad T=H+iK.
\]
Then $H^2=K^2=I$ and $HK+KH=0$. Hence Proposition \ref{4} gives
\[
 \omega_2(T)=\omega(T)=1.
\]
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{1}
Let $T=H+iK\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then
\[\omega_2(T)^2 \geq \frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert.\]
Equivalently,
\[\omega_2(T)^2 \geq \frac14\left\lVert T^*T+TT^*\right\rVert.\]
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Put
\[
A_\theta=\cos\theta H+\sin\theta K.
\]
Since $A_\theta=A_\theta^*$,
\[
\left\lVert A_\theta\right\rVert^2=\left\lVert A_\theta^2\right\rVert.
\]
By convexity of the operator norm, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega_2(T)^2
&=
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\left\lVert A_\theta^2\right\rVert\,d\theta\\
&\geq
\left\lVert 
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}A_\theta^2\,d\theta\right\rVert.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now,
\[
A_\theta^2
=
\cos^2\theta H^2
+\sin^2\theta K^2
+\sin\theta\cos\theta(HK+KH).
\]
Using
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta
=
\frac12,
\quad
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta
=
\frac12,
\]
and
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta=0,
\]
we obtain
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}A_\theta^2\,d\theta
=
\frac12(H^2+K^2).
\]
Thus
\[
\omega_2(T)^2\geq\frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert.
\]
Since
\[
H^2+K^2
=
\frac{T^*T+TT^*}{2},
\]
gives the second inequality.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
Let $T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then
\[\frac14\left\lVert T^*T+TT^*\right\rVert \leq \omega_2(T)^2 \leq \omega(T)^2.\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
Let \(T=H+iK\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)\). Then
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
\ge
\frac12\max\{\|H\|^2,\|K\|^2\}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{1}, we know that
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
\ge
\frac12\|H^2+K^2\|.
\]
Since \(H^2\ge O\) and \(K^2\ge O\), we have
\[
H^2+K^2\ge H^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
H^2+K^2\ge K^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\|H^2+K^2\|\ge \|H^2\|=\|H\|^2,
\]
and similarly
\[
\|H^2+K^2\|\ge \|K\|^2.
\]
Hence
\[
\|H^2+K^2\|\ge \max\{\|H\|^2,\|K\|^2\}.
\]
Combining this with Theorem \ref{1} gives
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
\ge
\frac12\max\{\|H\|^2,\|K\|^2\}.
\]
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The lower bound is sharp for self-adjoint operators. Indeed, if \(T=T^*\), then \(K=O\), and Proposition \ref{3} gives
\[
\omega_2(T)^2=\frac12\|T\|^2=\frac12\|H\|^2.
\]
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{6}
Let $T=H+iK\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then
\[\omega(T)^2 \leq \frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert+\frac12\sqrt{\left\lVert H^2-K^2\right\rVert^2+\left\lVert HK+KH\right\rVert^2}.\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Put
\[
A_\theta=\cos\theta\,H+\sin\theta\,K.
\]
Since $A_\theta$ is self-adjoint,
\[
\left\lVert A_\theta\right\rVert^2=\left\lVert A_\theta^2\right\rVert.
\]
Expanding the square gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_\theta^2
={}&
\cos^2\theta\,H^2
+\sin^2\theta\,K^2\\
&+\sin\theta\cos\theta\,(HK+KH).
\end{aligned}
\]
Use
\[
\cos^2\theta=\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2},
\qquad
\sin^2\theta=\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{2},
\]
and
\[
2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta.
\]
Then
\[
A_\theta^2
=
\frac12(H^2+K^2)
+
\frac12\cos2\theta\,(H^2-K^2)
+
\frac12\sin2\theta\,(HK+KH).
\]
Hence, by the triangle inequality,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lVert A_\theta\right\rVert^2
\leq{}&
\frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert\\
&+
\frac12|\cos2\theta|\,\left\lVert H^2-K^2\right\rVert\\
&+
\frac12|\sin2\theta|\,\left\lVert HK+KH\right\rVert.
\end{aligned}
\]
For nonnegative numbers $a$ and $b$,
\[
a|\cos t|+b|\sin t|
\leq \sqrt{a^2+b^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lVert A_\theta\right\rVert^2
\leq{}&
\frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert\\
&+
\frac12
\sqrt{
\left\lVert H^2-K^2\right\rVert^2+
\left\lVert HK+KH\right\rVert^2
}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the supremum over $\theta$ yields
\[
\omega(T)^2
\leq
\frac12\left\lVert H^2+K^2\right\rVert
+
\frac12
\sqrt{
\left\lVert H^2-K^2\right\rVert^2+
\left\lVert HK+KH\right\rVert^2
},
\]
as required.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
Let $T=H+iK\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then
\[\omega(T)^2\leq\omega_2(T)^2+\frac12\sqrt{\left\lVert H^2-K^2\right\rVert^2+\left\lVert HK+KH\right\rVert^2}.\]
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Let \(T=H+iK\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})\). The known estimate \cite[Theorem 1]{K2005}
\[
\omega(T)^2\le \frac12\|T^*T+TT^*\|
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\omega(T)^2\le \|H^2+K^2\|.
\]
On the other hand, Theorem \ref{6} states
\[
\omega(T)^2\le \frac12\|H^2+K^2\|+\frac12\sqrt{\|H^2-K^2\|^2+\|HK+KH\|^2}.
\]
Set
\[
S=\sqrt{\|H^2-K^2\|^2+\|HK+KH\|^2}.
\]
Then, Theorem \ref{6} gives
\[
\omega(T)^2\le \frac12\|H^2+K^2\|+\frac12 S.
\]
The two bounds coincide precisely when \(S=\|H^2+K^2\|\). In general, neither bound is uniformly better. Theorem \ref{6} is sharper when \(S<\|H^2+K^2\|\), whereas the known estimate is sharper when \(S>\|H^2+K^2\|\).

We illustrate both situations. First, let
\[
H=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1/\sqrt2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
K=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1/\sqrt2\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
H^2+K^2=I,\qquad
\|H^2-K^2\|=1,\qquad
\|HK+KH\|=1,
\]
so \(S=\sqrt2>1=\|H^2+K^2\|\). Theorem \ref{6} yields
\[
\omega(T)^2\le \frac{1+\sqrt2}{2}\approx 1.207,
\]
while the known estimate gives \(\omega(T)^2\le 1\). Here the known estimate is sharper.

Conversely, let
\[
H=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
K=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
H^2+K^2=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&5\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\|H^2+K^2\|=5,
\]
\[
H^2-K^2=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\|H^2-K^2\|=3,
\]
\[
HK+KH=\begin{bmatrix}0&3\\3&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\|HK+KH\|=3.
\]
Thus \(S=\sqrt{9+9}=3\sqrt2\approx4.243<5\). Theorem \ref{6} gives
\[
\omega(T)^2\le \frac{5+3\sqrt2}{2}\approx4.621,
\]
whereas the known estimate gives \(\omega(T)^2\le 5\). In this case Theorem \ref{6} is sharper.

Therefore, Theorem \ref{6} and the known estimate are complementary: neither one dominates the other in general.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{7}
Let $T=H+iK\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then
\[\omega_2(T)^2\leq\frac12\left\lVert H\right\rVert^2+\frac12\left\lVert K\right\rVert^2+\frac{2}{\pi}\left\lVert H\right\rVert\left\lVert K\right\rVert.
\]
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The result follows from
\[
\left\lVert \cos\theta H+\sin\theta K\right\rVert
\leq
|\cos\theta|\left\lVert H\right\rVert+|\sin\theta|\left\lVert K\right\rVert
\]
and the identities
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta
=
\frac12,
\]
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta
=
\frac12,
\]
and
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
|\sin\theta\cos\theta|\,d\theta
=
\frac1{\pi}.
\]
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
Let $T=H+iK\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then
\[\omega_2(T)\leq\frac{\left\lVert H\right\rVert+\left\lVert K\right\rVert}{\sqrt2}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
Let \(T=H+iK\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)\). Then
\[
\omega(T)^2
\le
\|H\|^2+\|K\|^2+\frac{4}{\pi}\|H\|\|K\|.
\]
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{5}, we have
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\omega(T)\le \omega_2(T),
\]
hence
\[
\omega(T)^2\le 2\,\omega_2(T)^2.
\]
By Theorem \ref{7}, we have
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
\le
\frac12\|H\|^2+\frac12\|K\|^2+\frac{2}{\pi}\|H\|\|K\|.
\]
Multiplying this inequality by \(2\) gives
\[
\omega(T)^2
\le
\|H\|^2+\|K\|^2+\frac{4}{\pi}\|H\|\|K\|.
\]
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Since \(\frac{4}{\pi}<2\), this bound is sharper than the classical estimate
\[
\omega(T)\le \|H\|+\|K\|,
\]
whose square is
\[
\|H\|^2+\|K\|^2+2\|H\|\|K\|.
\]
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{2}
Let $T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then for any unit vector $x\in\mathcal H$,
\[\omega_2(T)^2\geq\frac12|\left\langle Tx,x\right\rangle|^2+\frac12V_T(x).\]
Consequently,
\[\omega_2(T)^2\geq\frac12\omega(T)^2+\frac12\limsup_{n\to\infty}V_T(x_n),\]
for every sequence of unit vectors $(x_n)$ satisfying
\[
|\left\langle Tx_n,x_n\right\rangle|\longrightarrow \omega(T).
\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Set
\[
A_\theta=\cos\theta H+\sin\theta K.
\]
We have
\[
A_\theta x
=
(\cos\theta h_x+\sin\theta k_x)x
+
\cos\theta(H-h_xI)x
+
\sin\theta(K-k_xI)x.
\]
The first term is orthogonal to the other two terms because
\[
\left\langle (H-h_xI)x,x\right\rangle=0,
\qquad
\left\langle (K-k_xI)x,x\right\rangle=0.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left\lVert A_\theta x\right\rVert^2
={}&
(\cos\theta h_x+\sin\theta k_x)^2\\
&+
\left\lVert 
\cos\theta(H-h_xI)x+
\sin\theta(K-k_xI)x
\right\rVert^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Integrating the first term gives
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
(\cos\theta h_x+\sin\theta k_x)^2d\theta
=
\frac12(h_x^2+k_x^2).
\]
For the second term, the mixed term integrates to zero. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\left\lVert A_\theta x\right\rVert^2d\theta\\
&\qquad=
\frac12(h_x^2+k_x^2)
+
\frac12\left\lVert (H-h_xI)x\right\rVert^2
+
\frac12\left\lVert (K-k_xI)x\right\rVert^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since
\[
\left\lVert A_\theta\right\rVert\geq\left\lVert A_\theta x\right\rVert
\]
for every unit vector $x$,
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
\geq
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\left\lVert A_\theta x\right\rVert^2d\theta.
\]
Finally,
\[
h_x^2+k_x^2
=
|\left\langle Tx,x\right\rangle|^2.
\]
This proves the first assertion.

Now choose a sequence $(x_n)$ of unit vectors such that
\[
|\left\langle Tx_n,x_n\right\rangle|\to \omega(T).
\]
Apply the first assertion to $x_n$ and take the $\limsup$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
Let \(T=H+iK\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)\). If \(H\) and \(K\) commute, then
\[
\frac12\|H^2+K^2\|\le \omega_2(T)^2\le \|H^2+K^2\|.
\]
Moreover, if \(K=\lambda H\) for some \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) (or \(H=\lambda K\)), then
\[
\omega_2(T)^2=\frac12\|H^2+K^2\|=\frac14\|T^*T+TT^*\|.
\]
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The lower bound is Theorem \ref{1}. For the upper bound, since \(H\) and \(K\) commute, \(T=H+iK\) is normal. Hence
\[
\omega(T)=\|T\|.
\]
By Theorem \ref{5}, \(\omega_2(T)\le \omega(T)\). Therefore
\[
\omega_2(T)^2\le \|T\|^2=\|T^*T\|=\|H^2+K^2\|,
\]
because
\[
T^*T=(H-iK)(H+iK)=H^2+K^2+i(HK-KH)=H^2+K^2.
\]

Now suppose \(K=\lambda H\) for some \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\). Then
\[
\cos\theta H+\sin\theta K
=(\cos\theta+\lambda\sin\theta)H.
\]
Since \(H\) is self-adjoint,
\[
\|\cos\theta H+\sin\theta K\|
=|\cos\theta+\lambda\sin\theta|\,\|H\|.
\]
Thus
\[
\omega_2(T)^2
=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos\theta+\lambda\sin\theta|^2\,d\theta\,\|H\|^2.
\]
Using
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta
=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta
=\frac12,
\]
and
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta=0,
\]
we obtain
\[
\omega_2(T)^2=\frac{1+\lambda^2}{2}\|H\|^2.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
H^2+K^2=(1+\lambda^2)H^2,
\]
so
\[
\|H^2+K^2\|=(1+\lambda^2)\|H\|^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\omega_2(T)^2=\frac12\|H^2+K^2\|.
\]
Finally, since
\[
H^2+K^2=\frac{T^*T+TT^*}{2},
\]
the equivalent form follows.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
Let $T, S\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$. Then
    \begin{align*}
        \|T+S\|\leq 2 \sqrt{2} \omega_2\left(\begin{bmatrix}
            O & T\\
            S^* & O
        \end{bmatrix}\right)\leq \sqrt{2}(\|T\|+\|S\|),
    \end{align*}
    and the constant $2\sqrt{2}$ in the left side inequality is sharp.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let 
    $$\mathbb{M}=\begin{bmatrix}
          O & T\\
            S^* & O
    \end{bmatrix}\in \mathcal{B(H\oplus H)}.$$
    The cartesian decomposition of $\mathbb{M}=H+iK$ is given by $$H=\Re(\mathbb{M})=\frac{\mathbb{M}+\mathbb{M}^*}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}
          O & T+S\\
            T^*+S^* & O
    \end{bmatrix},$$ 
    and 
    $$K=\Im(\mathbb{M})=\frac{\mathbb{M}-\mathbb{M}^*}{2i}=\frac{1}{2i}\begin{bmatrix}
          O & T-S\\
            -(T^*-S^*) & O
    \end{bmatrix}.$$
    For $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, $\cos \theta H+\sin \theta K=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}
          O & e^{-i\theta}T+e^{i\theta}S\\
            e^{i\theta}T^*+e^{-i\theta}S^* & O
    \end{bmatrix}$.  Let us define $\mathbb{M}_\theta=e^{-i\theta}T+e^{i\theta}S$. So  $\cos \theta H+\sin \theta K=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}
        O & \mathbb{M}_\theta\\
        \mathbb{M}_\theta^{*}& O
    \end{bmatrix}$. \\
    Now,
    \begin{align*}
        \|\cos \theta H+\sin \theta K\|&=\left\|\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}
        O & \mathbb{M}_\theta\\
        \mathbb{M}_\theta^{*}& O
    \end{bmatrix}\right\|\\
    &=\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\|\\
    &=\frac{1}{2}\|e^{-i\theta}T+e^{i\theta}S\|\\
    &\leq \frac{1}{2}\left(\|T\|+\|S\|\right).
    \end{align*}
    Hence, for every $\theta$
    \begin{align*}
        \|\cos \theta H+\sin \theta K\|\leq \frac{1}{2}\left(\|T\|+\|S\|\right).
        \end{align*}
Now, integrating and squaring the above on both sides, we have
\begin{align*}
    \omega_2^2(\mathbb{M})=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\|\cos \theta H+\sin \theta K\|^2d\theta\leq \left(\frac{1}{2}\left(\|T\|+\|S\|\right)\right)^2. 
\end{align*}
Hence, 
\begin{align}\label{EqMatrix1}
    2\omega_2\left(\begin{bmatrix}
            O & T\\
            S^* & O
        \end{bmatrix}\right)\leq \|T\|+\|S\|.
\end{align}
Let us consider the following integral representation 
$$T+S=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos \theta~ \mathbb{M}_\theta d \theta.$$
Now take the norm on both sides
\begin{align}\label{EqnMatrix_2}
   \|T+S\|=\left\| \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos \theta~ \mathbb{M}_\theta d \theta\right \|\leq \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos \theta|\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\| d\theta. 
\end{align}
Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality 
{\small
\begin{align*}
            \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos \theta|\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\| d\theta\leq \left(\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 \theta d\theta\right)^{1/2} \left(\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\|^2d\theta\right)^{1/2}=\left(\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\|^2d\theta\right)^{1/2}.
\end{align*}
}
So \eqref{EqnMatrix_2} becomes 
\begin{align*}
   \|T+S\|\leq\left( \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\|^2 d\theta\right)^{1/2}. 
\end{align*}
We know from the definition of \emph{$L^2$-Cartesian numerical radius} of $\mathbb{M}$ by
\begin{align*}
     \omega_2^2(\mathbb{M})&=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\|\cos \theta H+\sin \theta K\|^2d\theta\\
     &=\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\|^2 d\theta\\
     &= \frac{1}{8\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\|^2 d\theta,
\end{align*}
which gives $\frac{1}{\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\|^2 d\theta=8\omega_2^2(\mathbb{M})$. 
So,
\begin{align*}
    \|T+S\|&\leq\left( \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\|\mathbb{M}_\theta\|^2 d\theta\right)^{1/2}\\
    &=\sqrt{8\omega_2^2(\mathbb{M})}=2\sqrt{2}\omega_2(\mathbb{M}).
\end{align*}
Hence \begin{align}\label{Eqnmatrix6}
    \|T+S\|\leq 2\sqrt{2}\omega_2\left(\begin{bmatrix}
            O & T\\
            S^* & O
        \end{bmatrix}\right)
\end{align}
       From \eqref{EqMatrix1} and \eqref{Eqnmatrix6}, we have 
        \begin{align*}
        \|T+S\|\leq 2 \sqrt{2} \omega_2\left(\begin{bmatrix}
            0 & T\\
            S^* & 0
        \end{bmatrix}\right)\leq \sqrt{2}(\|T\|+\|S\|).
    \end{align*}
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The constant $2\sqrt{2}$ in the left-hand inequality is sharp. To verify this, consider $\mathbb{M}=\begin{bmatrix}
        0 & 1\\
        1 & 0
    \end{bmatrix}$, where $T=S=1$, $\|T+S\|=2$, $\omega_2(\mathbb{M})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. So $2\sqrt{2}\omega_2(\mathbb{M})=2=\|T+S\|$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The classical numerical radius version of the inequality mentioned in the above theorem is known as the refinement of the triangle inequality (see \cite[Theorem 2.3]{KMY2015}).
    \begin{align*}
        \|T+S\|\leq 2 \omega\left(\begin{bmatrix}
            O & T\\
            S^* & O
        \end{bmatrix}\right)\leq \|T\|+\|S\|,
    \end{align*}
    for $T, S\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal H)$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
